title: Medical Insurance Claim Fraud Detection
summary:
Developed an end-to-end fraud-classification workflow over 10,000 synthetic medical claims, comparing five classifiers with feature engineering, training-only SMOTE, GridSearchCV, and stratified 60:20:20 validation.
Tuned LightGBM and selected a 0.25 decision threshold, increasing fraud recall from approximately 26% to 60.3% on an independent 2,000-claim test set while documenting the precision and false-positive trade-off.
Applied permutation importance and SHAP for global and claim-level explanations; reported F1, ROC-AUC, and PR-AUC and documented that the low-signal model is not production-ready.

data.canonical_name: Machine Learning-Based Medical Insurance Fraud Prediction
data.external_name: Medical Insurance Claim Fraud Detection - MSc Capstone

source_refs: context/sources/masters-projects.md > CAPSTONE PROJECT - Machine Learning-Based Medical Insurance Claim Fraud Detection
data.approved_external_use: Only for junior/graduate data-science or directly relevant analytics roles.
approved_facts: Built a supervised-learning workflow over a public synthetic dataset of 10,000 medical insurance claims, with an independent 2,000-record test set.
Engineered Claim Discrepancy and Delay Rate, compared five classifiers, and used a stratified 60:20:20 split with training-only SMOTE and a leakage-safe cross-validation pipeline.
Tuned LightGBM with GridSearchCV and selected a 0.25 probability threshold on validation data to improve fraud recall while explicitly accepting more false positives.

At the selected threshold, the independent test results were 60.3% fraud recall, 16.3% precision, 25.6% F1, 0.535 ROC-AUC, and 0.173 PR-AUC; the analysis concludes that discrimination is limited and not production-ready.
Applied permutation importance and SHAP for global and claim-level interpretation.
The MSc award remains in progress; final submission date and grade are not supplied.

summary:

Prevented future-information leakage by excluding the next-day close field and validated PCA suitability using correlation structure, Bartlett's test, and KMO 0.839.

title: Prototype Adjustment and DBSCAN Clustering
summary:
Implemented prototype-adjustment clustering, DBSCAN, and silhouette scoring from first principles and evaluated them on compact Gaussian and non-convex noisy datasets.
Compared three learning rates across 200 epochs, diagnosing slow convergence and overshooting; 0.05 provided the strongest speed/stability balance.
Achieved silhouette 0.814 with DBSCAN on Gaussian data and documented how epsilon selection fragmented the non-convex ring rather than overstating the result.

approved_facts: Implemented prototype-adjustment clustering, DBSCAN, and silhouette scoring manually on two reproducible synthetic datasets of 120 points each.
Compared learning rates 0.01, 0.05, and 0.20 across 200 epochs and found 0.05 provided the best speed/stability balance.
